Failure Scenarios: Inadequate Access Control of Distributed Energy Resources (DER) Systems Causes Electrocution
Description: DER owner fails to change the default password or not set a password for the DER system user interface. A threat agent (inept installer, hacker, or industrial spy) gets access through the user interface and changes the DER settings so that it does not trip off upon low voltage (anti-islanding protection), but continues to provide power during a power system fault
Relevant Vulnerabilities: V1A) Physical access may be obtained by unauthorized individuals to DER settings through the DER system user interface
Impacts: I1A) DER system suffers physical damage due to feeding into a fault
Potential Mitigations: M1A) Authenticate users for all user interface interactions
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.AC-7: Users, devices, and other assets are authenticated (e.g., single-factor, multi-factor) commensurate with the risk of the transaction (e.g., individuals’ security and privacy risks and other organizational risks)

Relevant Vulnerabilities: V1B) Default password is not changed for the DER system
Impacts: I1B) A utility field crew member may be electrocuted
Potential Mitigations: M1B) Change default access credentials after installation
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.AC-1: Identities and credentials are issued, managed, verified, revoked, and audited for authorized devices, users and processes

Relevant Vulnerabilities: V1C) System permits unauthorized changes to anti-islanding protection in the DER system due to poor configuration design
Impacts: I1C) The utility experiences damage to its reputation due to smart grid anomalies.
Potential Mitigations: M1C) Enforce limits in hardware so that no setting changes can damage equipment
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.DS-8: Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify hardware integrity

Relevant Vulnerabilities: V1D) Commands or other messages may be inserted on the network by unauthorized individuals between the user interface and the DER system, that result in unauthenticated changes to sensitive parameters.
Potential Mitigations: M1D) Train personnel on secure networking requirements so that DER owners will understand the impact of bypassing security settings
NIST CSF Subcategory:
PR.AT-2: Privileged users understand their roles and responsibilities
PR.AT-1: All users are informed and trained

Potential Mitigations: M1E) Require approval of next level of management for critical security settings.
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.AC-4: Access permissions and authorizations are managed, incorporating the principles of least privilege and separation of duties

Failure Scenarios:
DER’s Rogue Wireless Connection Exposes the DER System to Threat
Agents via the Internet
Description: An industrial or large commercial DER system is configured for local operational access through a wireless network, but is erroneously connected to the company’s wireless corporate network, thus exposing the DER system to the Internet. Through the incorrect connection to the Internet, a threat agent gains control of the DER system and alters the operation of the DER functions to make them ignore utility commands and to turn off the “acknowledge command” interaction with the utility. The DER system may no longer limit power output during critical situations.
Relevant Vulnerabilities: V2A) Network is connected to untrusted networks, specifically the DER operational network is connected to the company's wireless corporate network
Impacts:
I2A) Utility power equipment is damaged, causing financial impacts and outages of
customers
Potential Mitigations: M2A) Verify network changes including connections available between networks
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.DS-4: Adequate capacity to ensure availability is maintained

Relevant Vulnerabilities: V2B) System relies on credentials that are easy to obtain for access to the wireless network allowing an unauthorized entity to gain control of DER system through the Internet
Impacts: I2B) The utility experiences damage to its reputation due to smart grid anomalies
Potential Mitigations:
M2B) Authenticate devices so that any new connections support only authorized
equipment
NIST CSF Subcategory:
PR.AC-7: Users, devices, and other assets are authenticated (e.g., single-factor, multi-factor) commensurate with the risk of the transaction (e.g., individuals’ security and privacy risks and other organizational risks)
DE.CM-7: Monitoring for unauthorized personnel, connections, devices, and software is performed

Relevant Vulnerabilities: V2C) System permits wireless access by unauthorized parties to the wireless network in the DER system
Impacts:
I2C) The utility’s networked grid in a city may experience damaging reverse power
flows, or overloads to substation transformers
Potential Mitigations: M2C) Detect unauthorized configuration changes to the DER system
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.IP-3: Configuration change control processes are in place

Relevant Vulnerabilities: V2D) Unnecessary access is permitted to system functions in the DER system
Potential Mitigations:
M2D) Configure for least functionality by limiting the types of traffic, shutting down
certain ports, etc.
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.PT-3: The principle of least functionality is incorporated by configuring systems to provide only essential capabilities

Relevant Vulnerabilities: V2E) Users lack visibility to the failure of the system to respond to commands by the utility for the DER system
Potential Mitigations: M2E) Authenticate messages, including their source and destinations, in communication protocols used between DER system components
NIST CSF Subcategory:
PR.DS-6: Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify software, firmware, and information integrity
PR.PT-4: Communications and control networks are protected

Potential Mitigations: M2F) Require acknowledgements in communication protocols used for critical commands from the utility to DER systems
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.PT-4: Communications and control networks are protected

Potential Mitigations: M2G) Require failure messages in communication protocols used for critical commands from the utility to DER systems
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.PT-4: Communications and control networks are protected

Potential Mitigations:
M2H) Train personnel (DER system installers) to ensure that the recommended access
control security settings are enabled
NIST CSF Subcategory:
PR.AT-2: Privileged users understand their roles and responsibilities
PR.AT-1: All users are informed and trained

Potential Mitigations:
M2I) Require secure factory settings for configuration and network parameters by
default
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.IP-1: A baseline configuration of information technology/industrial control systems is created and maintained incorporating security principles (e.g. concept of least functionality)

Potential Mitigations: M2J) Authenticate users who make modifications to secure configuration and network parameters
NIST CSF Subcategory:
PR.AC-7: Users, devices, and other assets are authenticated (e.g., single-factor, multi-factor) commensurate with the risk of the transaction (e.g., individuals’ security and privacy risks and other organizational risks)
PR.IP-3: Configuration change control processes are in place

Potential Mitigations: M2K) Require approved cryptographic algorithms to protect DER wireless network
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.DS-2: Data-in-transit is protected

Potential Mitigations: M2L) Use Role-Based Access Control to limit privileges to safety critical functions
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.AC-4: Access permissions and authorizations are managed, incorporating the principles of least privilege and separation of duties

Potential Mitigations: M2M) Limit remote modification of functional and security settings for the DER system
NIST CSF Subcategory:
PR.MA-2: Remote maintenance of organizational assets is approved, logged, and performed in a manner that prevents unauthorized access
PR.AC-3: Remote access is managed

Failure Scenarios: Malware Introduced in DER System During Deployment
Description: A threat agent, possibly a disgruntled employee of the DER vendor or a DER implementation company, makes malicious software changes to equipment software or firmware. This malware causes large numbers of DER systems to ignore certain critical commands from the utility. For example, after some future date, it prevents the DER systems from limiting their energy output when so commanded and then locks out any other commands.
Relevant Vulnerabilities: V3A) Insiders with high potential for criminal or malicious behavior have access to critical functions or sensitive data when granted access to software and firmware in equipment that is at the vendor factory or during implementation
Impacts: I3A) Loss of a transformer
Potential Mitigations:
M3A) Cross check software/firmware before installation by comparing with a known
good version (a “gold disk”)
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.DS-6: Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify software, firmware, and information integrity

Relevant Vulnerabilities: V3B) System permits unauthorized installation of software or firmware in DER equipment
Impacts: I3B) Financial loss to utility
Potential Mitigations: M3B) Require on-going validation of software/firmware
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.DS-6: Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify software, firmware, and information integrity

Relevant Vulnerabilities:
V3C) System relies on credentials that are easy to obtain for access to modify software
or firmware on systems post-delivery
Impacts: I3C) Financial loss to DER owner
Potential Mitigations: M3C) Authenticate users for access to modify software/firmware
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.AC-7: Users, devices, and other assets are authenticated (e.g., single-factor, multi-factor) commensurate with the risk of the transaction (e.g., individuals’ security and privacy risks and other organizational risks)

Relevant Vulnerabilities: V3C) System permits unauthorized installation of software or firmware in the DER system
Impacts:
I3D) The combined effect causes a large reverse power flow in a substation and
causes severe damage to a substation transformer. All DER software/firmware
will have to be updated
Potential Mitigations: M3D) Verify personnel with background checks on DER development personnel, implementers, and contract maintenance personnel, especially those that interact directly with the DER interface to the utility
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.IP-11: Cybersecurity is included in human resources practices (e.g., deprovisioning, personnel screening)

Potential Mitigations: M3E) Use Role-Based Access Control to limit privileges to modify software/firmware after installation
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.AC-4: Access permissions and authorizations are managed, incorporating the principles of least privilege and separation of duties

Potential Mitigations: M3F) Test for malware in DER systems
NIST CSF Subcategory:
DE.CM-8: Vulnerability scans are performed
DE.DP-3: Detection processes are tested

Failure Scenarios: Confidential DER Generation Information Stolen to Harm Customer
Description: A utility is monitoring the energy and ancillary services provided by an industrial or commercial customer’s DER system. The communication protocol that transports this information is intercepted and a threat agent gains access to the private generation data from the DER system because the protocol provides either no confidentiality or inadequate confidentiality. This private data is used to harm the customer.
Relevant Vulnerabilities: V4A) System makes messages accessible to unauthorized individuals in the communication protocol of the DER system
Impacts: I4A) Utility is sued for financial damages due to lost customer privacy
Potential Mitigations: M4A) Encrypt communication paths used for confidential or private information
NIST CSF Subcategory:
PR.PT-4: Communications and control networks are protected
PR.DS-2: Data-in-transit is protected

Relevant Vulnerabilities: V4B) System makes private data accessible to unauthorized individuals in the communication protocol of the DER system
Impacts: I4B) Utility reputation is damaged for not providing security for private information
Potential Mitigations: M4B) Encrypt communication paths used for confidential or private information
NIST CSF Subcategory:
PR.PT-4: Communications and control networks are protected
PR.DS-2: Data-in-transit is protected

Failure Scenarios: Trojan Horse Attack Captures Confidential DER Generation Information
Description:
A DER system installed for the mutual benefit of a utility partnership with
an industrial or commercial customer contains a Trojan horse, either embedded at the
factory, added during installation, or inserted by maintenance personnel. The Trojan
horse captures confidential market-related information from both the utility and the
partner. An industrial competitor uses this market information to the detriment of both
the utility and the customer.
Relevant Vulnerabilities: V5A) System permits installation of malware in the supply chain for the DER system
Impacts:
I5A) Utility suffers from financial losses due to market manipulation by the industrial
competitor
Potential Mitigations: M5A) Test before installation of the DER system, for the presence of malware
NIST CSF Subcategory:
DE.CM-8: Vulnerability scans are performed
DE.DP-3: Detection processes are tested

Impacts: I5B) Utility is sued for financial damages due to lost customer confidentiality
Potential Mitigations: M5B) Test after installation of the DER system, for the presence of malware
NIST CSF Subcategory:
DE.CM-8: Vulnerability scans are performed
DE.CM-1: The network is monitored to detect potential cybersecurity events
DE.DP-3: Detection processes are tested

Impacts: I5C) Utility reputation is damaged for not being able to secure confidential information
Potential Mitigations: M5C) Require assured maintenance by security-certified maintenance organizations that can be trusted not to install malware
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.MA-1: Maintenance and repair of organizational assets are performed and logged, with approved and controlled tools

Potential Mitigations: M5D) Test after maintenance for malware in all DER systems
NIST CSF Subcategory:
DE.CM-8: Vulnerability scans are performed
DE.DP-3: Detection processes are tested

roles
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.PT-1: Audit/log records are determined, documented, implemented, and reviewed in accordance with policy

Potential Mitigations: M5F) Protect audit logs from deletion of records unless a security authority is notified
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.PT-1: Audit/log records are determined, documented, implemented, and reviewed in accordance with policy

Potential Mitigations:
M5G) Verify personnel with background checks on DER development personnel,
implementers, and contract maintenance personnel with privileges to modify
firmware or software
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.IP-11: Cybersecurity is included in human resources practices (e.g., deprovisioning, personnel screening)

Potential Mitigations:
M5H) Use Role-Based Access Control to limit privileges to modify firmware or software
after installation

Potential Mitigations: M5I) Restrict access at factory for modifying software and firmware
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.PT-3: The principle of least functionality is incorporated by configuring systems to provide only essential capabilities

Potential Mitigations: M5J) Require authentication to modify firmware or software after installation
NIST CSF Subcategory:
PR.MA-2: Remote maintenance of organizational assets is approved, logged, and performed in a manner that prevents unauthorized access
PR.IP-3: Configuration change control processes are in place

Potential Mitigations: M5K) Configure for least functionality by disabling backdoor vendor/maintenance ports
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.PT-3: The principle of least functionality is incorporated by configuring systems to provide only essential capabilities

Failure Scenarios: Compromised DER Sequence of Commands Causes Power Outage
Description:
A utility-owned DER storage system is located in a substation to balance large feeder generation and load variations. A threat agent causes a sequence of
commands, although valid individually, to arrive at the DER system in the wrong order (possibly through a replay attack), causing the DER system to create a greater imbalance and tripping off all customers served from that substation.
Relevant Vulnerabilities: V6A) System permits potentially harmful command sequences in the application-to application messaging scheme of the DER storage system
Impacts: I6A) Outages for all customers served by the substation
Potential Mitigations: M6A) Check message integrity in communication protocols used to manage DER systems
NIST CSF Subcategory:
PR.DS-6: Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify software, firmware, and information integrity
PR.PT-4: Communications and control networks are protected

Relevant Vulnerabilities:
V6B) A copy of a prior message or command is difficult or infeasible to distinguish from
a new legitimate message or command in the communication protocol of the DER storage system
Impacts: I6B) Continued threat of outages until the cause of the improper DER system operation is determined and corrected
Potential Mitigations: M6B) Protect against replay in communication protocols used to manage DER systems
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.PT-4: Communications and control networks are protected

Impacts: I6C) Utilities need to curtail customer generation and/or loads until the problem is corrected
Potential Mitigations: M6C) Create audit log of out-of-sequence data
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.PT-1: Audit/log records are determined, documented, implemented, and reviewed in accordance with policy

Potential Mitigations: M6D) Generate alarms for system owners when out-of-sequence data is detected
NIST CSF Subcategory: DE.AE-5: Incident alert thresholds are established

Failure Scenarios: Incorrect Clock Causes Substation DER System Shut Down During Critical Peak
Description: A utility-owned DER system is located in a substation with the primary purpose of providing additional power during a critical peak. A threat agent changes the time clock in the DER system through a false time-synchronization message, so that either the DER system believes that the critical peak event is over or that all timestamped messages to it are invalid, so it goes into default shut-down mode.
Relevant Vulnerabilities:
V7A) System permits messages to be modified by unauthorized individuals in the time
synchronization communication protocol
Impacts: I7A) The DER system performs an immediate shut down and causes damage to a transformer
Potential Mitigations: M7A)  Authenticate messages in the time synchronization communication protocol
NIST CSF Subcategory:
PR.DS-6: Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify software, firmware, and information integrity
PR.PT-4: Communications and control networks are protected

Relevant Vulnerabilities: V7B) Message modified by an adversary is either difficult or infeasible to distinguish from a valid message in the time synchronization communication protocol
Impacts: I7B) Customer outages occur during the critical peak
Potential Mitigations: M7B) Check message integrity in the time synchronization communication proto
NIST CSF Subcategory:
PR.DS-6: Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify software, firmware, and information integrity
PR.PT-4: Communications and control networks are protected

Relevant Vulnerabilities: V7C) System takes action before confirming changes with user in the DER management system
Impacts: I7C) Utilities need to curtail customer generation and/or loads until a new transformer is installed
Potential Mitigations: M7C) Cross check operationally critical actions with the utility DER management system before acting
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.DS-6: Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify software, firmware, and information integrity

Failure Scenarios: Electric Vehicle (EV) Charging Station Ignores Utility Command to Limit Fast-Charging
Description: A charging station employee (with system administrator authority) wants to increase the revenue of an EV charging station acting as a DER system. The employee modifies a utility command to “curtail the fast-charging rate” or to change the time-stamp when the fast-charging limit command was received. During a peak period, many EVs simultaneously start charging, causing the distribution transformer to fail.
Relevant Vulnerabilities: V8A) System permits unauthorized changes to instructions received from the utility regarding permitted charging operations
Impacts: I8A) Transformer is damaged
Potential Mitigations: M8A) Require read-only access to timestamps for stored copies of commands received from utility
NIST CSF Subcategory:
PR.IP-3: Configuration change control processes are in place
DE.AE-1: A baseline of network operations and expected data flows for users and systems is established and managed

Impacts: I8B) Lawsuits between the utility and the EV charging station over responsibility for the cost to replace the failed transformer
Potential Mitigations: M8B) Require non-repudiation for all critical commands between the utility and the customer system
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.DS-6: Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify software, firmware, and information integrity

Failure Scenarios: Loss of DER Control Occurs due to Invalid or Missing Messages
Description: A malicious or non-malicious individual causes the loss of DER control due to invalid or missing messages. Since the DER system either tries to act on invalid messages or no longer has messages constraining its output, it causes a distribution transformer to overload, thus causing an outage for the site and for neighboring sites. The DER system also sustains damage due to invalid settings
Relevant Vulnerabilities: V9A) System permits messages to be modified by unauthorized individuals
Impacts: I9A) A distribution transformer is damaged
Potential Mitigations: M9A) Authenticate messages in all communication protocols
NIST CSF Subcategory:
PR.DS-6: Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify software, firmware, and information integrity
PR.PT-4: Communications and control networks are protected

Relevant Vulnerabilities: V9B) Message modified by an adversary is either difficult or infeasible to distinguish from a valid message
Impacts:
I9B) A local outage occurs that requires field crews to replace the damaged
transformer
Potential Mitigations: M9B) Validate data in DER systems messages as reasonable and within the DER intrinsic capabilities
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.DS-6: Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify software, firmware, and information integrity

Impacts: I9C) The DER system may sustain damage due to trying to act on invalid messages or not being constrained by expected messages that did not arrive
Potential Mitigations: M9C) Generate alarms for messages that fail message authentication
NIST CSF Subcategory: DE.AE-5: Incident alert thresholds are established

Potential Mitigations: M9D) Create audit log of messages that fail message authentication
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.PT-1: Audit/log records are determined, documented, implemented, and reviewed in accordance with policy

Potential Mitigations: M9E) Require non-repudiation to validate receipt of messages
NIST CSF Subcategory: PR.DS-6: Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify software, firmware, and information integrity
